rows: Roof work should be avoided where the task can reasonably be completed without working at height.
All roofs should be treated as fragile until a competent person confirms otherwise.
Sloping-roof work normally requires suitable edge protection such as scaffolding.
Work on or near fragile surfaces requires a combination of stagings, guard rails, fall restraint, fall arrest or safety nets as appropriate.
Rooflights can be difficult to see and must be treated as potential fragile surfaces unless confirmed safe.
Short-duration maintenance and cleaning work still requires effective precautions.
Weather, wind, rain, ice and surface contamination must be considered before and during roof work.
Materials and tools must be controlled so they cannot fall from the roof or create trip hazards.
Roof material and age alone do not prove fragility, access safety or the adequacy of fall protection.
Safe methods depend on roof geometry, condition, duration, access, weather and rescue arrangements.
Construction businesses must conduct work without putting members of the public or other affected people at risk.
Site boundaries, adjacent land use, access routes and measures to exclude unauthorised people must be considered.
Physical fencing or hoarding should reflect the nature of the site and its surroundings.
Principal contractors must take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access.
Falling-object controls can include toe boards, brick guards, netting, fans or covered walkways.
Vehicle movements and deliveries must be arranged so pedestrians are not forced into danger.
Excavations, openings, plant, hazardous substances and stored materials must be secured when work stops.
Children, older people and people with disabilities may need additional protection and planning.
Public-risk controls depend on surrounding population, schools, roads, footpaths, access and the work phase.
A boundary map cannot verify fencing condition, visitor control, falling-object protection or current vehicle arrangements.
A safe system for work near underground services has three core elements: planning, locating and identifying services, and safe excavation.
Available plans should be obtained from relevant service owners before excavation begins.
Suitable locating devices should be used and detected service routes should be marked on the ground.
Plans and locating equipment should be supported by careful trial holes or other safe confirmation methods.
Workers must be briefed on service locations, uncertainties and the precautions required.
High-pressure gas pipelines identified on plans require consultation with the pipeline operator before work.
Safe digging practices should avoid uncontrolled mechanical excavation close to known services.
Services should be treated as live or hazardous until their status is reliably confirmed.
Service plans may be incomplete or inaccurate and usually do not guarantee exact depth or position.
Parcel or utility-map data cannot replace on-site detection, competent assessment and safe excavation controls.
Work-related contact dermatitis is skin disease caused or made worse by occupational exposure.
Repeated wet work and contact with irritants or skin sensitisers can damage the skin.
HSE promotes an Avoid, Protect and Check approach to managing work-related skin disease.
Exposure should first be avoided or reduced through substitution, process change or less-contact methods.
Suitable gloves and other controls must match the substance, task, duration and wearer.
Workers should wash contamination off correctly, dry the skin and use appropriate skin-care products.
Early signs can include dryness, redness, itching, cracking, blistering or swelling.
Health surveillance and prompt reporting can identify skin problems before they become severe.
Skin symptoms can have non-occupational causes and require competent clinical assessment.
Job title, premises type or product presence does not establish actual skin exposure or control effectiveness.
